neighboringSourceContext.speaker: Sam Harris
neighboringSourceContext.claimSummary: Multiple incompatible good lives do not eliminate moral truth because many paths can be good while others reliably produce misery.
neighboringSourceContext.reasonSummary: The moral-landscape metaphor permits many peaks yet preserves valleys, just as a question can have several right answers without making wrong answers disappear.

inferenceSummary.premise: There may be many distinct flourishing lives and societies, alongside conditions of profound misery.
inferenceSummary.inference: Plurality among successful answers is compatible with objective failure conditions.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Moral pluralism does not by itself imply relativism or defeat well-being-based truth.

neighboringSourceContext.reasonSummary: Earlier societies organized political labor around families and different roles, whereas modern politics treats individuals as the basic unit and lacks a good reason for exclusion.

neighboringSourceContext.speaker: Sam Harris
neighboringSourceContext.claimSummary: The anthropocentric boundary is too sharp because morality concerns every possible conscious mind and the experiences available to it.
neighboringSourceContext.reasonSummary: Future conscious computers and altered humans raise coherent questions about suffering and which intuitions to create; across such cases, holding other things constant, more misery is worse.

inferenceSummary.premise: Possible conscious systems can suffer even when their biology and intuitions differ radically from ours.
inferenceSummary.inference: The moral salience of worsening their experience does not depend on specifically human history or current convention.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Conscious experience supplies a wider and more stable basis for moral truth than anthropocentric practice.
